sections.text: You navigated the opening cleanly into a symmetrical pawn structure. After 8...Bb4+ 9.c3, you opted for 9...Ba5, which created a pin along the a5-e1 diagonal against the c3-pawn. Both sides developed smoothly until White established a knight outpost with 17.Ne5.

After trading knights on e5, retreating your knight with 18...Nd7 was a major misstep that gave White strong attacking chances. Rather than exploiting it, White played 19.e6, unleashing a discovered attack with their bishop on g3 against your bishop on c7. You captured with 19...fxe6, leaving the game sharp before it abruptly ended.

review.turning_point: When faced with 18.dxe5, retreating with 18...Nd7 put you under heavy pressure, whereas active central defense like 18...Ne4 was needed.
review.focus: Look for active central outposts rather than passive retreats when attacked by pawns, such as choosing 18...Ne4 over 18...Nd7.

review.headline: A sharp opening stumble in Petrov's Defense

sections.text: You stepped into a standard Petrov's Defense with 1...e5 and 2...Nf6, following the main lines up to 4...Nxe4. White chose an active approach with 5.Nc3, challenging your centralized knight immediately.

Instead of trading knights or retreating, you pushed 5...d5, and White seized the open e-file with 6.Qe2. Trying to hold everything together, you answered with 6...Qe7, but this created a fatal pin along the e-file that completely immobilized your knight on e4.

White exploited the pinned piece right away with 7.Nxd5, snapping up a pawn and attacking your queen. With your knight on e4 unable to help, you tried 7...Qe5, but facing massive material loss, the game was already over.

review.turning_point: The decisive moment arrived with 6...Qe7, which walked directly into a pin along the e-file and allowed White to break your center with 7.Nxd5.
review.focus: Be careful when dealing with an open e-file against an early enemy queen; instead of 6...Qe7, blocking the file with 6...Be7 avoids tactical pins.

review.headline: A sharp kingside push leads to a sudden queen trap

sections.text: Your opponent opted for the Blackburne Gambit with 2...c6, sacrificing a pawn to speed up their development. You accepted with 3.dxc6 Nxc6 and maintained a solid central grip with 4.Nf3 and 5.d4, neutralizing Black's initiative while keeping your material edge.

After developing smoothly, you decided to aggressively kick Black's light-squared bishop with 10.g4 and followed up with 11.h4. Pushing your kingside pawns before castling was a bit premature—developing naturally with 10.Nbd2 was cleaner—but it created immediate complications.

Black looked to exploit your uncastled king by grabbing the loose pawn with 11...Nxg4??, but moving the knight unleashed a discovered attack from your bishop on g5 against the undefended queen on d8. You immediately punished the oversight with 12.Bxd8!, leaving you up a full queen and prompting a quick resignation.

review.turning_point: Black's 11...Nxg4 completely overlooked that their queen was exposed to your dark-squared bishop, allowing 12.Bxd8 to win the game on the spot.
review.focus: Prioritize completing your development and securing king safety before launching flank pawn storms like 10.g4.

sections.text: The opening was a Petrov-style Three Knights game. You played 6...b6?! and 7...Bb7, and after 8.dxe5 grabbed with 8...Nxe4, which the engine did not like (8...Nxe5 was better). White replied with 9.exd6, and you played 9...Nxc3 (9...Nxd6 was the correct recapture).

You then missed chances with 16...Ng4 and 17...Bxg5, but White's 18.Ne7+ was a big blunder and 18...Bxe7! took the knight. From there you were up material and your rooks and knight did the rest, finishing with mate on move 46.

review.focus: Look at recaptures carefully: at 9...Nxc3 the engine preferred 9...Nxd6, keeping your pieces safe and developed.

review.focus: Before every move, check what the opponent's last move threatens. After 8...Nb4 the c2 square needed defending, and 9.Rc1 did that.

White made another mistake with 10.Nbd2, and you collected pawns with 10...Bxc2. After 13...Qd4, 14.Ne4 walked into 14...Qxe4!, which brought material to +7. You kept going with 15...Qb1+, 17...Qxb2 and 20...Qxd2, and the lead grew to around +12.

review.focus: Avoid loosening moves like 8...f6 when your pieces are exposed; 8...Nc6 developed and kept everything protected.

review.headline: Quiet Larsen opening, then a tactical blow-out where the opponent kept erring

sections.text: You went for the Nimzo-Larsen setup with 1.b3 and 3.g3, putting both bishops on the long diagonals. It was a slow, flexible start, and the engine felt Black was a shade more comfortable until the position opened up. Castling early and playing 7.Re1 followed by 9.e4 gave you a sensible center, and the trade on f3 left things level.

Your opponent then went wrong with 12...g6, which loosened the kingside and swung the evaluation to +4.1 for you. The engine liked 13.Qxf6 there, taking on the knight that guards Black's position. You chose 13.cxd4 instead, and the same idea was still on offer a move later with 14.Nd2 slipping again.

Black helped with 14...Bc5 (14...Bb4 was the better try), and after 15.Nc4 and 16.e5 your pieces were pointing at the king. 16...Nxe5 was another gift, and from 17.Nxe5 you were clearly ahead in material. 19.Nxf6 and 20.Qxb7 kept it going, and the trades at the end, 22.Rxe8 and 23.Bxe8, finished the job.
A win is a win, but you gave back a lot of advantage in the middle. Three times the engine's first choice was simply 13.Qxf6, 14.Qxf6 or 15.Qxf6, trading into a big edge.

review.turning_point: 12...g6 handed you +4.1, but 13.cxd4 let a lot of it slip; luckily Black kept making it worse with 14...Bc5 and 16...Nxe5.
review.focus: When the opponent weakens the king, look for the forcing queen capture first: at 13.cxd4 the engine wanted 13.Qxf6 straight away.

The opening had a few small inaccuracies. 6.Qf3 and 8.O-O-O were not the most precise, and 7.Bc4 pins the f7 pawn to the king, which was good in principle. But Black helped you with 6...e5 and then 8...Bxc3, a blunder that took the evaluation from +0.7 to +4.3.

You found the right recapture, 9.Bxc3, which also attacked the black queen on a5. After 9...Qb6 you played 10.dxe5, winning a pawn and opening the position, and your queen and bishop were both pointing at the black king's side.
10...Ng4 allowed 11.Qxf7#, the exclamation mark move: the bishop on c4 supported the queen and the king had no escape.

review.turning_point: 8...Bxc3 gave up the bishop pair, and 9.Bxc3 with tempo on the queen set up everything that followed.
review.focus: At 8.O-O-O the engine preferred 8.Qg3, which kept your king safe and still attacked the g7 pawn. Castling long walked into Black's bishop trade.

review.headline: A sharp kingside assault cut short by the clock

sections.text: You set up an aggressive posture early on, using 4.Qd2 and 5.Bh6 to trade off Black's defensive dark-squared bishop. Once your queen landed on h6 with 6.Qxh6, Black tried to push back on the queenside with 6...b5.

Your move 7.b3 was a mistake that let Black seize the initiative on the queenside, where pushing your attack with 7.h4 was much stronger. Black chipped away with 7...bxc4 8.Bxc4 Qa5, but they quickly cracked under pressure.

Black blundered with 9...e6, prematurely opening the center while their king was vulnerable. You calmly castled with 10.O-O and recaptured toward the center with 11.Nxd5 and 12.Bxd5, taking firm control before Black ran out of time on move 13.

review.turning_point: Black's blunder 9...e6 blew open the center right in front of your pieces, allowing you to seize a commanding position with 10.O-O.
review.focus: When you have a queen aggressively posted on the kingside, prioritize attacking pawn thrusts like 7.h4 over passive defensive moves like 7.b3.

review.headline: A sharp opposite-side castling battle slipped away on kingside defense

sections.text: With kings castled on opposite wings, both sides launched immediate flank pawn storms. You pushed forward on the queenside, but neglected central tension. Rather than locking things down or opening the center with 6...cxd5 7.cxd5, moves like 6...Qc7, 7...a5, and 8...a4 allowed White's attack on the kingside to strike first.

White crashed through with 16.gxf6 and 17.Nxh5, ripping open your king's shelter. After White played 22.Qh6+—pinning the knight on h7 to your rook on h8—you found the accurate retreat 22...Kf7! and grabbed counterplay against White's king with 21...Qxc3.

Under heavy fire, the defensive path narrowed. After White checked on g5, stepping forward with 23...Ke7?? walked straight into White's attack. White delivered 24.Qg7+ Kd8, and though 25...Kc7 set up a discovered attack on the h8-rook, your counter-checks ran out after 28...Qa1+ and White sealed the game with 36.Qxb5#.

review.turning_point: The critical mistake was 23...Ke7??, which stepped directly into a forced mate. Staying on the f-file with 23...Kf6 would have kept your king safe and maintained your counterplay.
review.focus: When under heavy flank attack, challenge the center early (such as finding 6...cxd5) rather than letting the opponent run their pawns freely down the board.

sections.text: You set up a solid fianchetto structure, but things quickly went wrong when you played 5...c5??. This allowed White to clamp down with 6.d5, leaving your d6-pawn backward and vulnerable. After White played 9.Nb5 and captured on d6 with 10.Nxd6, your response 10...Ne5?! set up a discovered attack along the d-file, but it still left you down a pawn and fighting for space.

White pushed your knights around with 13.f4 and 14.h3, exiling your piece to the rim with 14...Nh6. You found an active check with 19...Bc5+, but after 20.Be3, you retreated with 20...Bb4? instead of trading on e3. That gave White the tempo needed to launch a devastating pawn storm with 21.g4 and 22.g5, trapping your knight and forcing desperate defensive sacrifices.

After giving up an exchange with 22...Rxc6 23.dxc6 Qxc6, White still broke through by capturing your knight with 26.gxh6. With your kingside defenses stripped away and major pieces dominating the board, White swept in with 30.Qe6+ Kh8 31.Qxc8#.

review.turning_point: The critical mistake was 20...Bb4?, which handed White the initiative to play 21.g4 and trap your kingside knight.
review.focus: Be careful with opening pawn breaks like 5...c5?? that allow your opponent to lock up the center and target backward pawns.

The real damage came with 10...Rg8, which allowed 11.fxe6 and left you down material, with the evaluation around -6 after 11...Qxe6. You stayed active, though. 14...Nxh2 and 17...Rxg3 kept White's king under pressure.

review.focus: Look at 8...Nbd7: with White's pawn push on f4 hanging in the air, 8...exf4 was the simple way to keep your advantage.

review.headline: A Petrov where a bishop shot to h3 and left you far ahead, before the finish slipped

sections.text: This was a quiet Petrov with White playing slowly. White traded with 6.Bxf6 and you recaptured 6...gxf6, which doubled your pawns but opened the g-file. The engine marked the recapture as slightly inaccurate, yet 7...Rg8 put that open file to work straight away.

The game turned on 8...Bh3, which pins the g2 pawn against the rook on f1, so White could not simply take the bishop. White answered with 9.Nh4, and you found the best reply, 9...f5. That was a discovered attack: moving the pawn opened your e7 bishop onto the knight. 10.g3 then lost even more.

After 10...Bxf1 11.Bxf1 Bxh4 you were about five points up, and you kept it simple by trading queens with 14...Qxf5 15.exf5. The engine had you above +5 for most of the rest of the game, which is why your 93% accuracy is no surprise.
The one real slip came late, when you were low on time. At +6.2, 37...b3 let the evaluation fall to +3.9, and the game ended as a loss by resignation even though your side was still better.

review.turning_point: 9...f5 answering 9.Nh4 uncovered your bishop on the knight, and 10.g3 let the exchange win on f1 happen.
review.focus: With a big lead and little time, choose the simplest safe move. At 37...b3 the engine preferred 37...Rc2, which kept your winning edge intact.

review.headline: A sharp endgame squeeze decided by a sudden knight blunder

sections.text: You opened with the Scotch Game, and after early queen trades, Black went wrong with 5...Nxd8 instead of recapturing with the king. You missed the immediate 6.Nxe5, which would have snatched a clean central pawn, and instead chose 6.Bc4 to create a pin along the a2-g8 diagonal. Both sides castled and developed smoothly into a dry, balanced endgame.

You started targeting Black's structure by trading on d6 with 17.Nxd6 cxd6. After retreating your bishop, you went after the backward d6-pawn with 19.Bb4, setting up a pin on d6 against the rook. Black could have grabbed the e4-pawn, but stumbled with 19...Rfd8. You capitalized immediately with 20.Bxd6, winning a pawn and keeping up the pressure.

Things got tactical quickly when you pushed 22.h4. That gave Black the chance for 22...Nxf3+, forking your king and rook. Fortunately, your opponent missed it entirely and retreated with 22...Ne6. You didn't hesitate: 23.Bxe6 won the knight on the spot, forcing an immediate resignation.

review.turning_point: Black's fatal mistake 22...Ne6 missed the 22...Nxf3+ tactic and allowed you to play 23.Bxe6, winning a full piece.
review.focus: Look out for undefended central pawns right out of the opening; 6.Nxe5 instead of 6.Bc4 would have won material immediately after Black's early queen trade.

White cracked under the pressure when 26.Be2?? walked into trouble. After you rerouted with 26...Rh4, White panicked with 27.g3??, handing you a decisive advantage. Instead of 27...Qxe4+ 28.Bf3 Qxf3+, you played 27...Rxe4, which still kept you up a pawn. After 28.Bxh5 Qxf5 29.Qd3, 29...Qxh5 won a bishop but allowed White to untangle with 30.Qxe4.

Low on time, the game slipped away in the final moves. You tried the skewer 30...Bf5 against the queen and rook on b1, but after 31.Qxc6, you missed that your a8-rook was hanging. 31...Qg5?? allowed 32.Qxa8+, and White took the full rook with check.

review.turning_point: After winning White's bishop, playing 30...Bf5 allowed 31.Qxc6, which left your rook on a8 undefended and turned a winning game into a loss.
review.focus: Always check your own hanging pieces before launching counter-tactics, especially under time pressure as seen on 31...Qg5.

sections.text: You played 1.e4 and 2.d4 against the French, and Black's 2...h6 and 4...Na5? were slow. 4.Bc4?! and 5.Bb3?! lost some time as well, and after 6.Bd2 Bxd2+ 7.Nbxd2 and 8.e5?! the game was fairly level.

You missed it again on 13.Ne4??, when 13.Rxa6 was still available. After 13...Bxc4 14.bxc4 and 14...Nb4? you stayed in the game: 15.O-O-O Na2+? 16.Kb1! was the accurate reply, and the knight had to go back with 16...Nb4.
In the last phase 18.f4?! and 19.h4? were pushed without finishing the plan (19.d5 was the engine suggestion), and 20.h5?? again missed 20.d5. Black ran out of time first and you took the win.

review.focus: Look for captures first. On 12.Qg4?? and 13.Ne4?? the rook on a1 could simply take on a6 with 12.Rxa6, and the same on move 13.

8.Qf3? was a small inaccuracy: 8.Bd5 was the sharper move, but it still worked because Black greedily took with 8...bxc3?? (8...e6 was needed).

sections.text: 1.Nf3 d5 2.d4 Bg4 3.e3 is a sensible set-up for you, and 3...f6?! (engine suggestion: 3...e6) loosened your king side a little, but it was only a small inaccuracy (-1.0). After 4.c4 e5 5.dxe5 fxe5 you grabbed the centre, and 7...Bxe2 8.Qxe2 traded off your active bishop.

8...Qg5?! (the engine liked 8...Qd6) invited trouble but the real mistake was White's: 9.Ng4?? attacked your queen but hung the knight, and you found 9...h5!, which hit it again. After 10.h4 Qxg4 11.Qxg4 hxg4 you were a clean knight up (+4.7).

13...Rxh4?! was a slight inaccuracy (13...Nf6 was a cleaner move), but you continued calmly. 16.Ng3? was another White slip and you found 16...Bxg3! to trade a strong piece and open the position further.

From then on you kept the initiative: 17...Ne4 centralised the knight, 19...axb4 and 22...Nxd5 took pawns, and you finished with the rook trade 31...Rxf4+. White's king walked into the centre and you won on time.

review.turning_point: 9.Ng4?? gave away the game; 9...h5! swung it from -0.5 to +4.2.
review.focus: Build your pawn structure first: 3...f6?! weakened the e6 and g6 squares for no gain, so 3...e6 would have developed with fewer risks.

sections.text: A Four Knights Italian started normally, but 5.Nxe5?? was a trick that does not work: after 5...Nxe5 6.d4 Nxc4 you were behind (-2.4). Quieter moves such as 5.d3 kept everything safe.

Black then went wrong. 9.Nd5?! looked risky but set a trap, and 9...dxc5?? fell for it. You found 10.Nxf6+!, a knight check that also unveiled your queen on d1 against the queen on d8 (a discovered attack). After 10...gxf6 11.Qxd8+ Kxd8 12.Bxf6+ and 13.Bxh8 you had won back everything and more (+4.8).

From there you simply played good chess: you castled long, pushed with h4 and g4, and used the open files for your rooks. 27.Bxe7 and the h-pawn run to 35.h8=Q showed clean technique, and you won on time.

Two moments cost you a faster finish. On 40.Qe2+? the engine had a forced mate in two with 40.Re4 c4 41.Qd5#. On 48...Kc5 Black erred and 49.Kc3? missed 49.Re3, again with a mating attack available. Neither changed the result.

review.focus: Check forcing moves before simplifying: on 40.Qe2+? you had 40.Re4 and a forced mate, and on 49.Kc3? you had a similar mating line. Also avoid 5.Nxe5, which gave up a piece for a pawn.

review.headline: A Colle game decided early by 7...Qb6?? and a series of missed chances to hit back

sections.text: White set up a Colle with Nf3, e3, Bd3 and Nc3, and you built a sound Queen's Gambit-style position. The problem came at 7...Qb6??. After 7.e4 the engine wanted 7...dxe4, when the pawn on e4 attacks both the bishop on d3 and the knight on f3 (a fork). Instead 8.e5 won space, 9.exf6 removed your defender and you were clearly worse (-5.0).

You kept fighting. 11...Bxc3! was the best reply to White's 11.a3?, and 14.Nxe5?? was an error by White, but 14...Re8?? missed the point: 14...Qxe5 would have taken the knight and kept your queen active. After that the attack on g6 and h6 gave White the upper hand again.

White went wrong too, with 17.Qh6?? and 19.Rbd1??, and you found 19...Qg7!, a good defensive resource. The next big moment was 22...Bh5??; the engine pointed to 22...Qxh6 as the stronger move. Then 23.g4?? gave you one more chance, and 23...Nf3+ (a fork of the king on g1 and rook on e1, as well as a discovered attack on the e-file) was the answer. 23...Nf7?? let it slip.
After the queens came off on 24.Qxg7+ you made it to a long endgame, but 33...Nc5 (instead of 33...gxh5) lost more ground, and White converted.

review.turning_point: 23.g4?? gave you the position back and 23...Nf3+ was crushing; 23...Nf7?? let White off the hook instead.
review.focus: Look at checks and captures first. On 23...Nf3+ the knight forks the king on g1 and rook on e1, and on 22...Qxh6 you simply had a strong capture available instead of retreating with 22...Bh5??.

sections.text: You answered 1.e4 with ...e5 and ...d5, trading into a comfortable game. 6...a6 and 7...b5 grabbed queenside space but loosened your pieces, and White's 9.Bg5? was a genuine mistake. You found the best reply, 9...f6!, and later 11...h5! also hit the right note after 11.Bg3 gave you a big edge.

The trouble was that you handed the advantage back. 10...g5 was a blunder that let White off the hook, and 13...Bc5 was the next slip; the engine preferred 13...Qd7. After 14.d4 e4? you lost a pawn to 16.Rxe4+ and were suddenly the one defending (-2.0).

You fought back well. 20.Rxe7?? was a blunder by White, and 20...Nxe7! was the right recapture: the knight left d5 and uncovered your bishop on b7 against the knight on f3, a discovered attack that left you well ahead.

21...Nd5? let some of that evaporate (21...g4 was stronger), and 23...Nxb4?? swung the evaluation from +1.5 to -2.5. Then 26...Qc5?? walked into 27.bxc5 and cost you the queen. The game ended on the clock, though the position was already lost.

review.turning_point: 23...Nxb4?? turned a healthy +1.5 into -2.5; 23...Rde8 kept everything protected. 26...Qc5?? then finished the job.
review.focus: Before each queen move, check which pawns attack the destination square: on 26...Qc5 the pawn on b4 simply took it. 26...Qd5 would have hit the queen on f5 and the knight on b3 at once (a fork).

6.Nf7?? forked the queen and rook, but the king captured it and you lost a piece for little (-3 in material). The engine preferred 6.Qh5+ g6 7.Nxg6. Luckily 8...g6?? came next and 9.Bc4+! put you back at +6.6.

After 10.Bxd5+ Kg7 you were doing well (+7.1), but 11.b3?? threw it away. The engine's 11.Qe5+ would have set up a skewer on the king and rook, and after your opponent's 11...Bb4+?? your 12.Kf1?? passed up 12.Qxb4, which would have won a piece.
You still had a forced win after 13.Bb2+, 14.Qf4+ and 15.Qf7. The final blunder was 20.f3+??, because 20.Qh3# was checkmate, and the game ended with a loss on time.

review.turning_point: 20.f3+?? missed 20.Qh3#, a checkmate that would have won the game on the spot.
review.focus: At 20.f3+ you missed 20.Qh3#; when you have a big attack, look for forcing moves like checks that finish the game.

review.headline: A French Exchange win built on a poorly timed queen check

sections.text: You chose the Exchange French with 2.d4 and 3.exd5 exd5, then developed with 4.Nc3. After 4...c5 you played 5.Nf3?!, and the engine preferred 5.dxc5 d4, but it was not a big concession.
5...Qe7+?? was the mistake that decided the game. You found 6.Be3!, blocking the check and keeping your pieces working, and after 6...cxd4 7.Bb5+ Bd7 8.Nxd4 you were already clearly better (+2.8).
8...Bxb5? traded off the bishop on your terms: 9.Ndxb5 recaptured and left you with two active knights (+4.3). Your opponent should have played 8...Nf6.
From there 9...Nc6 10.Nxd5 Qe5 11.Nbc7+ brought both knights into the attack and won a pawn along the way, and your opponent resigned after 11...Kd7.

review.turning_point: 5...Qe7+?? was a premature check, and 6.Be3! blocked it and left you clearly better.
review.focus: At 5.Nf3 the engine preferred 5.dxc5; when the opponent's pawn challenges your centre, consider taking it before developing.

sections.text: You met the Center Game calmly with 2...exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qd1 Nf6 5.Nc3 Bb4 6.Bd2 Bxc3 7.Bxc3, and the position was healthy. Your 7...Nxe4?! was a pawn grab that the engine rated at -0.4; castling with 7...O-O first was the quieter option.

Your opponent's 8.Bd3?? was the blunder; 8.Qg4 would have kept things balanced. You found the best answer, 8...Nxc3!, and after 9.bxc3 you came out a clean pawn up and followed with 9...O-O to finish development.
10.Nf3 Re8+ 11.Be2 Qe7 12.O-O Qxe2 picked up a bishop and put you well ahead (+5.0). 13.Qd5 Qxc2 won another pawn, and your queen was dominating the board.

You finished in style: 14...Qg6 and 16...Ne7 kept your pieces coordinated, 17.f5 Qxg5 took the knight, and 19.Qxc7 Bxf5 added another pawn. After 22.Qc6 you took the queen with 22...bxc6, and the game ended on time.

review.turning_point: 8.Bd3?? allowed 8...Nxc3!, which broke White's structure and left you a pawn ahead with the better pieces.
review.focus: At 7...Nxe4 the engine preferred 7...O-O; take a moment to castle before grabbing material in the opening.

sections.text: You played the French with a normal 2.d4 and 3.Nf3 setup, and 4.Nc3 dxe4 5.Nxe4 Nf6 6.Bd3 Nxe4 7.Bxe4 f5 left you slightly better (+1.9 after 7...f5). Your development with 9.Bg5, 10.Qd2 and 11.Be3 was sensible.

The first mistake was 12.Bxh6??. After 12...gxh6 13.Qxh6 you had two pawns for the bishop, and the engine's 12.O-O-O would have kept your edge. The sacrifice looked attractive but there was no follow-up that worked.
After 13...Rf6 14.Qg5+ Kf8 you kept the initiative, but 15.Ne5?? dropped you to -2.7 because 15...Qxd4 was strong. Your opponent missed it with 15...Nd7.
16.Ng6+?? Kf7 17.Nf4 left you still worse, but 17...c5?? let you back to level (0.0). The game ended on time after 17 moves, so keep an eye on the clock.

review.turning_point: 12.Bxh6 gave a bishop for two pawns when you were already doing well, and the attack that followed ran out of steam.
review.focus: At 12.Bxh6 the calm 12.O-O-O kept your edge; before sacrificing, count whether your next two moves create real threats.

The decisive moment was 13.Nc4??. After 12.O-O Bc5, your opponent's knight went to a square where 13...Bxc4! just took it, and you were up a piece (+5.5).

sections.text: You answered 1.d4 with a solid 1...d5 and developed with 2...Nf6 and 3...Nc6. White pushed with 6.e5, and 6...Nd7?! was the one slightly passive moment; 6...Nd5 was more active. Still, you got your pieces out with 7...e6 and stayed calm.
Your opponent then overreached. 8.d5?? opened lines, and 8...exd5! was the right capture. After 9.Qxd5 Qe7 10.Bg5 f6 11.Bh4 Ndxe5 you had won a pawn and your pieces were well placed.
12.Bc4?? walked into the best shot in the game: 12...Nxc4+! was a discovered check from your queen along the e-file, and the knight took the bishop at the same time. It put you far ahead, up four.
You kept converting accurately: 13.Kd1 Be6 14.Re1 Rd8 15.Rxe6 Qxe6 and then 16...Qxd5 picked up the queen. The finish with 21...Rd3, 22...Qxc3+ and 24...c6# was clean.

review.headline: A calm Scandinavian grind with a well-timed trap on the bishop

sections.text: You met the Scandinavian with 3.Nc3 and 4.Qe2, which allowed the queen trade after 4...Qxe2+ 5.Ngxe2. It was a small inaccuracy (4.Be2 was the engine's choice), but the endgame was comfortable for you and you developed steadily with 6.f3, 7.d4 and 8.Bf4.

The key structural decision was 10.Bxa6 bxa6, which wrecked your opponent's pawns, followed by 11.O-O-O. After 13...Bf4? you struck with 14.Nxd5!, taking the knight, and the exchanges that followed left you +1.8.
Then came the highlight. 17...Bc4?? put the bishop on a square where 18.b3! trapped it, and after 18...Bb5 19.axb5 axb5 you were a piece for a pawn ahead. Very good spotting.

From there it was technique: 21.Rde2 and 22.Rxe2 traded a pair of rooks, then 24.Rxg7 and 25.Rxh7 picked up pawns. You missed a quicker finish, though. 26.Rh8+ Re8 27.Rxe8# was a back rank mate, and the same idea worked a move later with 27.Rg8+ Re8 28.Rxe8#.

review.focus: At 26.Rg7 you had a back rank mate with 26.Rh8+ Re8 27.Rxe8#; in winning positions, check every forcing move before improving slowly.

sections.text: An Italian Game where you opened the centre with 4.d4 and 5.dxe5?!, then slipped with 7.Nbd2?. The engine preferred 7.Nxe5, a discovered attack that would have won a piece, so that was the chance you missed in the opening.

The middlegame was tactical. After 8.h3 Bxf3 9.Nxf3 Nxe4 10.Bf4 Nxf3+ 11.Bxf3 d5 12.Qe2 Qa5+ you played 13.Bd2??, and that was your one big error: the bishop was pinned to your king by the queen on a5, which left a piece to be won.
Your opponent missed it with 13...Bb4?, since 13...Qxd2+ was available. You then found 14.c3!, and 14...Bxc3?? gave you the chance to recapture with 15.Bxc3!, hitting the queen with tempo.
From there you converted cleanly. 16.Bxe4 won a piece, and after 17.O-O dxe4 18.Qxe4 you stayed well ahead. 20.Rad1 and 21.Rd7 piled up the pressure before 22.Qxe2 ended it.

review.focus: At 7.Nbd2 you passed on 7.Nxe5, which would have won a piece; before developing, check whether an enemy piece is loose.

review.headline: A sharp central battle slipped away after a loose piece was left hanging

sections.text: You set up a solid center against the Modern Defense, but tension peaked early on e5. After 8.Bxe5, setting up a pin along the diagonal toward h8, Black traded on e5. Recapturing with 9.Nxe5? lost a central pawn to 9...Qxd4. However, after 10.Nxc6, Black let you back into the game with 10...Qxd1+, allowing 11.Rxd1! to regain balance.

The game was decided in a single tactical misstep. After Black kicked your knight with 12...f5, you tried counter-attacking with the pin 13.Bb5, but it simply left your knight undefended. Black snapped it off with 13...fxe4, leaving you down a piece before the clock ran out.

review.turning_point: 13.Bb5?? gave away a full piece to 13...fxe4 because the knight on e4 was completely unprotected.
review.focus: When your opponent attacks a piece with a pawn, move the attacked piece to safety instead of creating counter-threats that fail to protect it, as happened on 13.Bb5.

sections.text: You expanded on the queenside early and castled long, though opening the center with 14...cxd3 and 15...Qxd3 left your queen exposed. White immediately cracked with 16.Qb3??, allowing you to win the queen with 16...Bxb3!.
Up massive material, you pushed toward White's king. White pressured your rooks, but you broke through on f2 to deliver checkmate on g1.

review.turning_point: White blundered their queen on 16.Qb3??, and you took it immediately with 16...Bxb3! to take a decisive lead.
review.focus: Look for intermediate captures before grabbing pawns; 15...Bxa2 was much stronger than 15...Qxd3.
